370.t: Meeting Alfred Lion at Jimmy Ryan's
370.s: Berton took her to 52nd Street and Jimmy Ryan's, where he introduced her to Alfred Lion and Frank Wolff.
370.ch: Alfred Lion and early Blue Note
370.q: Well, I can thank Ralph Berton for that, because he was playing Blue Note records on the air. Nobody else in this whole town ever played them. He played the 10-inch and the 12-inch. I was fascinated by those records alone. I would sometimes come in to New York from New Jersey with a girlfriend,…

370.t: Alfred Lion's background and the Lexington Avenue office
370.s: Alfred fled Germany with a big record collection, partnered with Frank Wolff, set up Blue Note offices and gave her albums of his records.
370.ch: Alfred Lion and early Blue Note
370.q: Alfred was brilliant. He was European. He left Hitler’s Germany, thank goodness, and came to New York, and he had a huge jazz record collection that he brought with him from Berlin. He lived over on First Avenue. He acclimated himself very quickly. He got a lot of buddies around him. He bought…

370.t: Frank Wolff and the First Avenue apartment
370.s: While Alfred was in the Army, Wolff kept Blue Note going; Gordon describes the pair's close friendship and their record-filled apartment.
370.ch: Alfred Lion and early Blue Note
370.q: Oh, well, Frank Wolff, who was the buddy he brought from Germany to New York apparently... Their friendship was so intense that I didn’t need a mother-in-law. I mean...no, they weren’t gay or anything. You know, Europeans have a different kind of male friendship than Americans have with men. They…

370.s: Ike Quebec was Blue Note's first musician friend and guide into Black jazz circles; he brought along Art Blakey.
370.q: Oh, yeah. What a dear man. Ike was I think the first friend that Blue Note Records really had as a musician and a friend. Most musicians were pals, but Ike was a friend. He was dear. And we loved his playing, because Alfred recorded him constantly, and I swooned because he had that great big sax…

143.t: Alfred Lion invites him to record for Blue Note
143.s: Lion approached him at Minton's and asked if he could play like Parker, and he said yes.
143.q: Yeah, but that was later on. But then, I don’t really know whether Ike was with him or not. But he came up to me and said, “Oh, do you want to record for Blue Note?” Well, you know I’m going to tell him “yeah.” He said, “But you’ve got to play like Charlie Parker. Can you play like Charlie Parker?”…

143.t: Bringing Blue Mitchell and Horace Silver to Blue Note
143.s: He heard Mitchell with Lloyd Price and found Horace Silver practicing at Newman's, and brought both to the label.
143.q: I met him...he was working with Lloyd Price’s band, and I heard him, and he sounded so beautiful. I said, “Man, I got to get you a date.” So he came on over to the Blue Note. See, a lot of people don’t know, I brought Horace over there, too.

426.t: Gil Melle and how Alfred Lion came to Rudy for Blue Note
426.s: Gil Melle's album led Alfred Lion to bring Rudy his next Blue Note recording after his WOR engineer sent him to the maker of the sound.
426.q: Well Gil Melle recorded for Gus first, as far as I know. He had a band, played saxophone, he was a really great guy too. He sold that to Alfred Lion, who released that on Blue Note. So, Alfred wanted to make another album, so he took the first one that I had made, and took it to the engineer. At…

65.t: Howard McGhee and Brew Moore on "Cubop City"
65.s: Machito says Roost label partners Teddy Reig, Morris Levy and Symphony Sid paired McGhee and Moore against the complicated rhythm.
65.ch: Mambo, the Palladium and Cubop City
65.q: Well, in those days, Howard McGhee was in his best and Brew Moore start coming up very strongly. He played very nice and ......

385.t: Ike Quebec and the Blue Note session
385.s: Blue Note arranged for him to record with Ike Quebec, a friend from Atlantic City.
385.ch: Chords, recordings and his own groups
385.q: ... The studio, Blue Note, arranged that we record together, but he and I knew each other, we used to hang out together -- went to Atlantic City. He was a good friend, man. We got things together and had a good session...

412.t: Alfred Lion, Francis Wolff and the Village aficionados
412.s: Hodes explains that Alfred Lion and Frank Wolff were part of the Village aficionado scene, along with the Ertegun brothers.
412.ch: Radio, Jazz Record and Blue Note (Reel 2)
412.q: Alfred Lion? Well, Alfred Lion again was part of the aficionado scene. Alfred Ljon and Frank Wolff. They were both also in that Village scene, as was in part the Turkish ambassador's Ertegun sons, You could see their faces now and then.

170.t: Lee Morgan's first date for Blue Note with Alfred Lion
170.s: Philly Joe brings Ware to the Blue Note date with Lee Morgan and Horace Silver; Alfred Lion starts calling him.
170.ch: Riverside and the New York scene
170.q: And I was ... like I say, I was kind of established now, recording with everybody during this period, and one day Philly Joe Billy Joe grabbed me one day and said, "Man, come over here to the Blue Note, and make this date with Lee Morlin and Horace Silver and Billy and myself -- it was Lee's first…
